article.title: How Many Bottles of Wine Per Person at a Wedding?
article.body:
How Many Bottles of Wine Per Person at a Wedding?

Plan on half a bottle of wine per adult guest for the meal, which is about three 125ml glasses each, and three-quarters of a bottle if the celebration runs from the ceremony into the evening. For 100 guests that means 50 to 75 bottles. Drinks House 247 suggests counting only the adults who will be drinking.

Wedding drinks are one of the few parts of the budget where both running out and over-ordering feel expensive. The good news is that the maths is predictable once you fix two numbers: how much each glass holds, and how long people will be drinking.

Where does the half-a-bottle rule come from?

A standard 75cl bottle pours six glasses of 125ml, the standard small measure for wine in the UK. Over a sit-down wedding breakfast of two to three hours, most guests who drink wine have two or three glasses. Three glasses is half a bottle, which is why half a bottle per drinking guest is the planning figure caterers and venues use most often.

If the day carries on into an evening reception with dancing, consumption continues but slows. Adding a further quarter of a bottle per guest covers most evenings, bringing the total to three-quarters of a bottle, or four to five glasses per person across the day.

How much wine for your guest count?

The table below assumes every counted guest is an adult who drinks wine, and 125ml glasses.

Drinking guests Meal only (½ bottle each) Full day (¾ bottle each) Champagne for one toast glass each
3015 bottles23 bottles5 bottles
5025 bottles38 bottles9 bottles
7538 bottles57 bottles13 bottles
10050 bottles75 bottles17 bottles
15075 bottles113 bottles25 bottles
200100 bottles150 bottles34 bottles

The toast column assumes one full 125ml glass per guest, six to a bottle. If the toast pour is smaller, around 75ml, one bottle stretches to about ten glasses.

Who should you leave out of the count?

The fastest way to over-order is to multiply by the full guest list. Before you do the sums, take out:

  • Children and anyone under 18.
  • Guests who do not drink alcohol, including those who are driving. Plan good non-alcoholic options for them instead.
  • Guests who mainly drink beer or spirits. If you are running a bar as well as serving wine, reduce the wine figure by the share of guests you expect to head there.

For a guest list of 120 with 15 children, 10 non-drinkers and a busy beer bar, the real wine-drinking count might be closer to 80 than 120.

How should you split red, white and rosé?

A half-and-half split between red and white is a sensible starting point, then adjust for the day itself:

  • Summer or outdoor weddings: lean towards white and rosé, perhaps 60% white and rosé to 40% red.
  • Winter weddings or rich menus: lean towards red.
  • Fish or vegetarian main course: more white.
  • Beef or lamb main course: more red.

Choose wines that are easy to like rather than challenging. A wedding is not the place for a wine that divides opinion. A fresh, dry white, a soft and fruity red and a crisp rosé cover almost every palate.

What about the drinks reception and toast?

If you serve a glass of fizz on arrival, plan for guests to have one or two glasses during a reception of about an hour. That adds a third to half a bottle of sparkling wine per drinking guest, on top of the wine for the meal. Some couples serve the same fizz for the reception and the toast; others switch to champagne only for the toast. Our guide to how much champagne you need for 50 guests works through the fizz maths in detail.

Practical points that change the numbers

  • Glass size. If your venue pours 175ml, a bottle gives only four glasses. Ask the venue what measure its staff use and adjust the maths.
  • Top-ups. Waiting staff who top up glasses constantly raise consumption. Ask for glasses to be refilled on request rather than automatically.
  • Corkage. If you supply your own wine, check whether the venue charges corkage per bottle, as it affects which wines make sense.
  • Chilling. White, rosé and sparkling wine need to be cold. A bottle chills in 20 to 30 minutes in a bucket of ice and water, but dozens of bottles need space and plenty of ice arranged in advance.
  • Returns. Some suppliers accept unopened bottles back after an event. Check this before ordering rather than assuming.

When should you order?

Order the wine once your final numbers are confirmed, usually two to four weeks before the day, and have it delivered with enough time to chill. Our guide to how far in advance to order wine for a wedding covers the timing in detail.

Frequently asked questions

How many bottles of wine do you need per person at a wedding?

Plan on half a bottle per adult drinking guest for the meal, which is about three 125ml glasses. If the celebration runs into an evening reception, allow three-quarters of a bottle per guest.

How much wine do I need for 100 wedding guests?

For 100 adults who drink wine, plan on about 50 bottles for the meal, or 75 bottles for a full day and evening. Remove children, non-drinkers and beer drinkers from the count first.

Should I order more red or white wine for a wedding?

Start with half and half. Lean towards white and rosé for a summer or outdoor wedding or a fish main course, and towards red for a winter wedding or a beef or lamb main course.

How many glasses of wine are in a bottle?

A 75cl bottle pours six 125ml glasses, five 150ml glasses or four 175ml glasses. Check which measure your venue uses before you do the maths.
